Mar 05, 2026 at 08:00 PM EST
Hamadeh backs Mullin as ‘right leader’ for DHS
Arizona Republican Abe Hamadeh offered strong support for Senator Markwayne Mullin’s nomination to lead the Department of Homeland Security, telling Newsweek he believes Mullin is well-suited for the job. Hamadeh said his experience working alongside Mullin gives him confidence in the senator’s ability to take on the department’s top role at a moment of intense scrutiny.
He added that Trump “knows how to pick a winning team” and noted that Arizona sits on the front lines of national‑security and border‑security challenges. Hamadeh said he looks forward to continuing to work with Mullin as he transitions into the position.
Mar 05, 2026 at 07:46 PM EST
Noem’s FEMA bottlenecks helped trigger her removal
Kristi Noem’s firing came after months of mounting anger over her decision to personally review every FEMA contract and grant over $100,000 — a policy that slowed reimbursements communities had been waiting on for months or even years. The delays drew bipartisan frustration, culminating this week in sharp criticism from lawmakers who said disaster‑stricken regions were being left in limbo.
Rep. Kevin Kiley pressed Noem on a $2.5 million wildfire‑mitigation grant that had cleared every approval except her signature, telling her his constituents “are not being well served.” Similar complaints had been building in North Carolina, where recovery from Hurricane Helene stalled until senators forced Noem to release long‑delayed funds.
Disaster‑relief experts said they hoped aid would finally move faster after her dismissal. Rafael Lemaitre, a former FEMA official, called the firing “long overdue,” arguing that communities need an agency focused on safety rather than political interference.
Mar 05, 2026 at 07:30 PM EST
DNC chair says Noem’s exit highlights ‘chaos’ inside Trump administration
Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin issued a blistering statement following Kristi Noem’s removal as homeland security secretary, calling her departure overdue and emblematic of deeper turmoil within the Trump administration. Martin said Noem’s tenure “was a disaster for the American people,” accusing her of overseeing unconstitutional enforcement tactics that traumatized communities, detained young children, and resulted in the deaths of two U.S. citizens in Minnesota.
He also charged that Noem misused public funds, describing DHS under her leadership as a “slush fund” that supported her personal lifestyle rather than public safety. Martin argued that the problems extend far beyond a single official, saying the administration is “in freefall” and that personnel changes alone cannot repair the damage.
Mar 05, 2026 at 07:16 PM EST
DelBene says Noem’s firing is only the start of needed accountability at DHS
Representative Suzan DelBene said Kristi Noem’s removal as homeland security secretary marks a necessary but insufficient step toward restoring safety and oversight at the Department of Homeland Security. In a statement released Thursday, the Washington Democrat said Noem’s tenure was defined by deadly failures, citing the killings of innocent Americans and what she described as violent ICE operations that spread fear in communities across the country.
DelBene said the public has been demanding accountability for months and stressed that “it doesn’t stop with one firing.” She called for stronger legal safeguards and more aggressive congressional oversight to prevent abuses and ensure DHS operates within the law. According to DelBene, meaningful reform will require structural changes, not just a change in leadership.
Mar 05, 2026 at 07:02 PM EST
Rep. Magaziner says Noem’s firing follows a year of ‘dysfunction’ at DHS
Representative Seth Magaziner delivered a sharply critical assessment of Kristi Noem’s tenure after her removal as homeland security secretary, telling Newsweek that the department had “plunged into dysfunction” under her leadership. In an exclusive comment, he accused Noem of overseeing a period marked by deadly enforcement failures, mismanagement, and politically driven decision‑making.
Magaziner pointed to the killings of two American citizens by DHS agents and a series of high‑profile ICE operations that he said terrorized communities rather than targeting individuals with criminal records. He argued that Noem’s enforcement priorities swept up vulnerable people—including veterans, pregnant women, and children with serious illnesses—while failing to impose accountability for agents’ actions.
He also criticized what he described as the erosion of DHS’s core national‑security functions, saying Noem “gutted” cybersecurity and counterterrorism capabilities and mismanaged FEMA during a period of heightened disaster risk. Magaziner further cited no‑bid contracts awarded to Noem's associates as evidence of deeper ethical and operational breakdowns.
Mar 05, 2026 at 06:49 PM EST
Jewish Council for Public Affairs says Noem’s exit doesn’t fix deeper DHS problems
The Jewish Council for Public Affairs said Kristi Noem’s removal as homeland security secretary does little to address what it views as systemic failures inside the Department of Homeland Security. In a statement, CEO Amy Spitalnick argued that Noem oversaw “dangerous policies” but warned that the issues run far deeper than any single official.
Spitalnick said DHS has “militarized immigration enforcement” in ways rooted in dehumanizing conspiracy theories, leading to civilian deaths and repeated violations of U.S. law. She also criticized the department for delaying critical security funding for synagogues and other vulnerable institutions through the Nonprofit Security Grant Program, while adding political conditions that she said forced communities to choose between safety and their values.
According to the organization, these problems reflect structural choices rather than individual missteps. Spitalnick said Congress must use its funding and oversight powers to ensure transparency and accountability, regardless of who leads the department, arguing that meaningful reform will require sustained pressure from lawmakers.
Mar 05, 2026 at 06:35 PM EST
Immigrant-rights group says Noem’s firing is ‘bare minimum,’ calls for accountability at DHS
Mi Familia Vota sharply condemned former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem’s tenure following her removal, arguing that her leadership left a trail of abuses and fear across immigrant communities. In a statement, President and CEO Héctor Sánchez Barba said Noem “leaves DHS in disgrace,” citing deaths in federal custody and the fatal shootings of U.S. citizens Alex Pretti and Renée Good by DHS agents. He accused Noem of misleading the public about those incidents and presiding over an enforcement strategy that traumatized families nationwide.
Sánchez Barba said ICE operations under Noem amounted to a “reign of terror,” alleging that raids, detentions, and aggressive tactics left parents afraid to take children to school and sick individuals hesitant to seek emergency care. He argued that Noem not only oversaw these actions but actively championed them, framing her removal as an overdue response to systemic harm.
But the organization stressed that firing Noem does not constitute meaningful reform. Sánchez Barba said the American public deserves a Department of Homeland Security that protects rather than endangers communities, and pledged to closely monitor DHS secretary‑designate Markwayne Mullin. He said the group intends to hold the incoming leader accountable “every single day,” just as it did with Noem, to ensure the department upholds safety, transparency, and respect for civil rights.
Mar 05, 2026 at 06:21 PM EST
Schiff highlights Noem’s contradictory testimony after sudden firing
Senator Adam Schiff pointed to a sharp discrepancy between Kristi Noem’s sworn testimony and her abrupt removal as Homeland Security Secretary, noting that she told lawmakers this week that Trump personally approved a $220 million public‑relations contract awarded to the spouse of her former communications aide.
Mar 05, 2026 at 06:06 PM EST
Senate blocks test vote to fund DHS as shutdown drags on
The Senate failed to advance a procedural vote on a Department of Homeland Security funding measure, prolonging the partial shutdown that has left the agency without full operational authority.
The test vote fell short 51–45, well below the 60 votes needed to move the bill forward, underscoring the deep partisan divide over immigration enforcement and DHS oversight.
Mar 05, 2026 at 05:53 PM EST
Senate could confirm Mullin on party-line vote as DHS scrutiny intensifies
Senator Markwayne Mullin is positioned to win confirmation as the next homeland security secretary with only Republican votes, a shift made possible by the Senate’s simple‑majority threshold for executive nominees. While Democrats could slow the process through procedural maneuvers, they cannot block it outright unless GOP support fractures. Some Republicans may also see the moment as an opportunity to extract concessions or spotlight concerns about the department’s direction.
Traditionally, nominees for major national‑security posts receive broad deference from colleagues, an informal courtesy that smooths the confirmation process. But Mullin may face a tougher path. The Department of Homeland Security is under intense scrutiny following months of controversy, congressional investigations, and public anger over enforcement operations. Senators from both parties have signaled that the next secretary will be expected to answer for the department’s conduct and outline a credible plan to restore stability.
Mar 05, 2026 at 05:40 PM EST
Officials offer blunt assessments of Noem’s tenure after her removal
Reactions from current and former immigration‑enforcement officials paint a sharply mixed picture of Kristi Noem’s leadership following her removal as secretary of homeland security. One current ICE official, speaking anonymously to allow candid comment, told Newsweek he had no personal criticism of Noem but believed she had become a political lightning rod. “I don’t know her that well… I’ve never met her in person, and I just know that she has a target on her back,” he said.
Others were far more direct. Thaddeus Cleveland, the Republican sheriff of Terrell County, Texas, described Noem as “flashy and toxic,” arguing that DHS accomplishments over the past year occurred “in spite of, not because of, her leadership.” He accused her of micromanaging agencies, deploying resources for political rather than operational reasons, and lacking meaningful experience in border or immigration enforcement. Cleveland said DHS now needs a leader capable of managing a sprawling national‑security department amid heightened global instability.
Darius Reeves, who retired in 2025 as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations field office director in Baltimore, echoed that sentiment. He said Noem’s removal “was coming,” adding that she routinely embarrassed the agencies she oversaw and failed to match the professionalism of her predecessors.
Mar 05, 2026 at 05:27 PM EST
CHIRLA says Noem’s removal must be followed by major DHS reforms
The Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA) welcomed the announcement that Kristi Noem has been removed as Secretary of Homeland Security, calling her departure “long overdue” after what the group described as a tenure marked by chaos, abuses, and a lack of accountability. In a statement from Executive Director Angelica Salas, the Los Angeles–based immigrant‑rights organization said recent congressional hearings underscored systemic failures under Noem’s leadership, including policies that treated immigrant families “as targets rather than human beings.”
Salas said Noem’s exit should be viewed only as an initial step toward repairing the department’s credibility. As President Donald Trump prepares to appoint a new DHS secretary, CHIRLA urged the administration to choose someone committed to lawful, transparent governance and to restoring dignity in the treatment of immigrant and refugee communities. The group called for an end to what it described as a culture of impunity within agencies such as ICE, CBP, and USCIS, arguing that meaningful reform requires stronger oversight and respect for constitutional protections.
CHIRLA emphasized that immigrant communities expect a fundamental shift in approach—one grounded in accountability, transparency, and basic human respect. The organization said the next DHS leader must prioritize safety and fairness over fear‑driven enforcement, noting that trust cannot be rebuilt without structural changes within the department.
Mar 05, 2026 at 05:12 PM EST
What is Markwayne Mullin’s relationship with Trump like?
Senator Markwayne Mullin’s nomination to lead the Department of Homeland Security comes after years of cultivating a notably close relationship with President Donald Trump, one that has positioned him as a trusted political ally and behind‑the‑scenes adviser. Mullin was among the Republicans who backed Trump’s false claims that the 2020 election was stolen, aligning himself early with the former president’s most loyal faction and reinforcing his standing within Trump’s inner circle.
Inside the Senate, Mullin became known as a conduit between congressional Republicans and the White House. Senate Majority Leader John Thune once described him as a “Senate whisperer” for Trump—someone who could translate legislative realities to the president and, at times, steer his decision‑making. That role expanded during Trump’s 2024 campaign, when Mullin served as a key surrogate tasked with outreach to Indigenous voters in battleground states, a constituency he worked to mobilize through targeted events and messaging.
Mar 05, 2026 at 04:59 PM EST
What to know about Markwayne Mullin’s MMA career
Before entering national politics, Oklahoma Senator Markwayne Mullin built a brief but undefeated career in professional mixed martial arts, a chapter that continues to shape public interest in his background.
Competing between 2006 and 2007, Mullin logged a spotless record—listed as either 5–0 or 3–0 depending on how early regional bouts were recorded—while drawing on a lifetime of wrestling experience and a black belt in Brazilian jiu‑jitsu.
His athletic résumé later earned him induction into the Oklahoma Wrestling Hall of Fame in 2016.
Mar 05, 2026 at 04:46 PM EST
Watchdog group says Noem’s exit won’t fix DHS without policy shift
American Oversight said Kristi Noem’s departure as homeland security secretary does little to address what it describes as a deeper crisis inside the Department of Homeland Security, arguing that the problems stem from White House‑driven policies rather than any single official. In a statement responding to President Donald Trump’s plan to replace Noem with Oklahoma Senator Markwayne Mullin, Executive Director Chimoma Chukwu said the administration’s immigration agenda has relied on “abusive and inhumane tactics” that will continue unless the underlying directives change.
Chukwu warned that a new secretary will inherit agencies already facing scrutiny over detention conditions, civil‑rights concerns, and use‑of‑force incidents. The group said the central issue is not personnel but the policy framework that has shaped DHS operations, describing it as one that prioritizes secrecy and political messaging over transparency and public safety. According to the statement, “swapping out one political appointee for another” will not restore trust without a clear break from practices that have “cost lives and eroded public confidence.”
American Oversight said the public deserves clarity about how DHS policies are being carried out and called for greater accountability as the department transitions to new leadership. The organization, which uses public records requests and litigation to investigate government misconduct, said meaningful reform will require the administration to abandon the approach that has defined its enforcement strategy to date.
Mar 05, 2026 at 04:33 PM EST
Jayapal says Noem’s firing must be followed by structural DHS reform
Representative Pramila Jayapal said Kristi Noem’s removal as homeland security secretary is overdue but insufficient, arguing that Congress should not approve new funding for the Department of Homeland Security until there is clear evidence of major internal reform. In a statement shared with Newsweek, Jayapal said she had called for Noem to be “fired, to resign, or to be impeached,” and described the department under Noem as “lawless,” citing a series of high‑profile controversies that intensified scrutiny of DHS operations.
Jayapal pointed to the deaths of two U.S. citizens during immigration enforcement actions, the detention of children and families, and what she described as the wrongful detention of American citizens as examples of systemic failures. She also referenced reports of 41 deaths in DHS custody and criticized the department’s spending decisions, including multimillion‑dollar advertising campaigns that drew bipartisan concern in Congress. Her statement framed Noem’s departure as a necessary step but emphasized that the underlying issues extend far beyond a single official.
Jayapal said Congress “cannot fund DHS” until there is “real, tangible proof” that the administration is committed to meaningful structural change.
Mar 05, 2026 at 04:23 PM EST
Mullin says DHS nomination is the honor of his career
Senator Markwayne Mullin said his nomination to lead the Department of Homeland Security marks the greatest privilege of his 13 years representing Oklahoma in Congress. In a statement, he reflected on his roots in Westville and thanked President Trump for appointing him to lead the department after Kristi Noem’s firing.
Mar 05, 2026 at 04:20 PM EST
Advocacy group says Noem’s removal marks a ‘people-powered victory’
Common Cause is celebrating what it calls a major win for government accountability after the removal of Kristi Noem as Secretary of Homeland Security, crediting a nationwide grassroots effort that pushed for her ouster. The organization said its “Fire Kristi Noem” campaign mobilized tens of thousands of Americans in response to what it described as a pattern of corruption, misuse of power, and fatal enforcement abuses during Noem’s tenure.
Virginia Kase Solomón, the group’s president and CEO, said Noem’s departure reflects public refusal to accept a department “weaponized against the very people it’s sworn to protect.” She pointed to the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti during federal operations as emblematic of what the organization views as systemic failures under Noem’s leadership. Common Cause said its campaign gathered nearly 100,000 petition signatures, generated tens of thousands of calls to Congress, and deployed high‑visibility tactics—including digital ads and a mobile billboard near the White House and DHS headquarters—to pressure the administration.
The group stressed that Noem’s firing is only a first step, arguing that DHS remains in crisis and should not receive additional funding until a leader committed to public safety and accountability is in place. Common Cause said it will continue pressing for a moratorium on ICE operations in local communities and for full cooperation with investigations into the Minneapolis shootings that intensified scrutiny of Noem’s leadership.
Mar 05, 2026 at 04:06 PM EST
Newsom criticizes Mullin’s appointment after Noem’s firing
California Governor Gavin Newsom sharply criticized President Donald Trump’s decision to appoint Senator Markwayne Mullin as the next Secretary of Homeland Security, pointing to a series of past controversies involving the Oklahoma Republican. In a statement on X, Newsom highlighted several incidents from Mullin’s public record, including a moment in which he appeared unable to recall whether the U.S. was engaged in military conflict, as well as his state’s comparatively high violent‑crime rates.
He also referenced a heated exchange during a Senate hearing in which Mullin confronted union workers and told one to “shut your mouth,” along with a separate hearing where Mullin said, “I don’t want reality” during a discussion on race.
Newsom argued that these episodes raise concerns about Mullin’s temperament and readiness to lead the Department of Homeland Security, calling him “erratic” and “unstable” as he questioned the administration’s judgment in elevating him to the post.
Mar 05, 2026 at 03:52 PM EST
Newsom calls for broader accountability after Noem’s removal
California Governor Gavin Newsom issued one of the strongest reactions yet to the dismissal of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, arguing that her firing should mark the beginning—not the end—of a wider reckoning inside the Department of Homeland Security. In a statement, Newsom said Noem would be remembered as “the most shamelessly incompetent and cruel Homeland Security Secretary in U.S. history,” and insisted that removing her from office “is not enough.”
Newsom called for additional scrutiny of senior DHS figures, naming Greg Bovino and White House policy adviser Stephen Miller as officials he believes should also face accountability for what he described as policies that “terrorized and endangered the American people.”
Mar 05, 2026 at 03:38 PM EST
Replacement rumors swirled leading up to Kristi Noem’s ousting
President Donald Trump announced on March 5, 2026, that he will replace Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem with Oklahoma Senator Markwayne Mullin at the end of the month, ending a period of mounting controversy and speculation surrounding Noem’s future in the administration. Her removal follows a series of political and operational challenges that had increasingly strained her standing inside the White House.
Noem’s leadership had come under scrutiny on several fronts. Senior officials were reportedly frustrated with what they viewed as slow progress on expanding detention capacity, a key priority of the administration’s immigration agenda. Her position weakened further after two days of contentious congressional hearings, where lawmakers from both parties pressed her on a $220 million taxpayer‑funded advertising campaign that prominently featured her and bypassed standard contracting procedures.
The turbulence was compounded by persistent rumors about an alleged relationship between Noem and longtime adviser Corey Lewandowski—claims both have denied but which nonetheless created political discomfort for the White House. Internally, aides, including Deputy Chief of Staff for Policy Stephen Miller, were said to be pushing for a leadership change, with former Virginia Governor Glenn Youngkin briefly considered as a possible successor.
Despite public assurances from the White House in late 2025 that Noem’s job was secure, speculation continued to build until her removal was formally announced in early March. Trump said Noem will transition into a new diplomatic role as special envoy for The Shield of the Americas, a hemispheric security initiative launching this month. Mullin, a Republican senator and member of the Cherokee Nation, will take over DHS on March 31 as the administration seeks to reset its approach to immigration enforcement and internal management.
Mar 05, 2026 at 03:28 PM EST
Mullin says DHS nomination was only ‘a little bit of a surprise’
Senator Markwayne Mullin said his selection to lead the Department of Homeland Security was not entirely unexpected, though the timing caught him off guard. Speaking with reporters at the Capitol, the Oklahoma Republican said he had long maintained a close relationship with President Donald Trump, describing the two as “great friends” and expressing enthusiasm about joining the cabinet.
Mullin also emphasized his personal regard for outgoing Secretary Kristi Noem, calling her “a friend” and noting he had not yet spoken with her since the announcement. He defended her performance, saying she was handed an extraordinarily difficult portfolio and “performed the best she can do” under the circumstances.
Mar 05, 2026 at 03:24 PM EST
Schumer and Warren say Noem’s firing exposes deeper problems at DHS
Senate Democratic leaders reacted sharply to the removal of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, arguing that her dismissal highlights broader concerns about the Department of Homeland Security’s conduct and the administration’s handling of immigration enforcement. Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer said Noem’s exit should not be seen as a resolution to the controversies surrounding DHS, calling her departure overdue but emphasizing that “the problems at DHS go much deeper than any one person.” He urged the administration to rein in Immigration and Customs Enforcement and address what he described as ongoing violence tied to federal enforcement operations.
Senator Elizabeth Warren focused on the circumstances surrounding Noem’s firing, pointing to the scrutiny she faced over a more than $200 million advertising campaign that prominently featured her. Warren questioned why the president acted only after Noem’s testimony about the ads, noting that he did not intervene following the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens during immigration operations in Minneapolis.
Mar 05, 2026 at 03:10 PM EST
Noem accused of steering ICE contract as Trump announces her exit
Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem personally selected the firms behind a $100 million Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruitment campaign, bypassing the competitive bidding process normally required for federal contracts, according to internal communications and three administration officials. The documents show Noem and her aides pushed the work to two politically connected companies despite warnings from career staff that other bidders could do the job for less.
In one August exchange, then–ICE deputy chief of staff Madison Sheahan reprimanded an employee for suggesting alternative contractors, telling him the award was “a decision made by the secretary,” according to internal messages. The employee was later called into Sheahan’s office and scolded for “overriding” Noem before ultimately agreeing to direct the contract to the firms she favored, officials said. The campaign, launched in late fall, aimed to hire 10,000 new ICE officers through targeted ads, hiring events, and outreach to veterans and gun owners.
A DHS spokesperson said the ICE director’s office made the contracting decisions and that the approach allowed the agency to quickly expand its workforce. But the officials familiar with the process said acting ICE Director Todd Lyons was not involved and that the directive originated with Noem.
The revelations come as Noem’s standing in the administration had already eroded following the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens during immigration operations in Minneapolis, tensions with the U.S. Coast Guard, and testimony this week that angered President Donald Trump. On Thursday, Trump announced she would step down on March 31 and transition to a new diplomatic role as special envoy for the administration’s “Shield of the Americas” initiative. He named Oklahoma Sen. Markwayne Mullin as her successor.
Noem also faced bipartisan scrutiny over a separate $220 million ad campaign that prominently featured her. She told lawmakers the president approved the ads, but Trump told Reuters he “never knew anything about it,” deepening questions about her management of DHS and the political messaging efforts she oversaw.
Mar 05, 2026 at 03:05 PM EST
Noem embraces new envoy role after sudden DHS exit firing
Kristi Noem publicly welcomed her reassignment to a newly created diplomatic post on Thursday, thanking President Donald Trump for appointing her as special envoy for the Shield of the Americas and highlighting what she described as major achievements during her 13‑month tenure leading the Department of Homeland Security. Her statement marked her first response since Trump announced he would replace her with Oklahoma Senator Markwayne Mullin at the end of the month.
Noem framed the envoy position as a continuation of her national‑security work, saying the Western Hemisphere is “critical for U.S. security” and that she plans to work closely with senior administration officials on efforts to disrupt narcotics trafficking networks. She cast her time at DHS as a period of historic progress, citing border enforcement metrics, deportation figures, child‑location efforts, and disaster‑relief timelines, as well as internal cost‑saving measures and Coast Guard modernization.
Mar 05, 2026 at 02:57 PM EST
Noem avoids any mention of firing in Nashville appearance
Kristi Noem spoke for more than 20 minutes at a Nashville law‑enforcement conference on Thursday, delivering a full policy‑focused address even as news of her removal as Homeland Security Secretary was breaking in real time. Appearing before the Sergeant Benevolent Association’s Major Cities Conference, she made no reference to Trump’s decision to replace her at the end of the month. Audience members who later posed questions also avoided the topic, creating a striking disconnect between the unfolding political moment and the event inside the room.
Noem instead discussed immigration enforcement, federal‑state cooperation, and grant funding, speaking as though she remained firmly in her role. When asked about future support for law‑enforcement agencies, she pointed to DHS terrorism‑related grants and suggested she would continue facilitating access to them. “Maybe what I’ll do is I will forward those grant opportunities to all of you so that you can share them with your departments,” she said, offering guidance that implied continuity rather than imminent departure.
Mar 05, 2026 at 02:56 PM EST
California Sen. Ted Lieu says public pressure helped force Noem’s removal
California Senator Ted Lieu said Wednesday that public protest and congressional oversight played a decisive role in President Donald Trump’s decision to remove Kristi Noem as Secretary of Homeland Security. In a statement, Lieu thanked demonstrators who documented what he described as “horrific abuses” carried out by masked DHS agents under Noem’s leadership, arguing that their recordings helped expose misconduct that might otherwise have remained hidden.
Lieu pointed to two high‑profile oversight hearings held this week by the House and Senate Judiciary Committees, where lawmakers from both parties pressed Noem on allegations of excessive force, mismanagement, and misuse of federal authority. He said the testimony and evidence presented during those sessions revealed a pattern of “corruption and abuse of power,” culminating in Trump’s decision to dismiss her from the post.
Mar 05, 2026 at 02:43 PM EST
What is the Shield of the Americas?
The Shield of the Americas is the Trump administration’s new hemispheric security initiative, created as part of a broader effort to reshape U.S. engagement in Latin America. The administration has made the Western Hemisphere a central foreign‑policy priority, framing the region as part of the United States’ “immediate sphere of influence” and elevating an “Americas First” approach. The initiative emerges at a moment when the administration has withdrawn from several regional organizations and postponed the traditional Summit of the Americas, signaling a shift away from large multilateral forums toward smaller, ideologically aligned partnerships.
The Shield of the Americas is being launched through a summit in Miami with a select group of right‑leaning Latin American leaders. The document notes that those invited represent “the recent right‑ward shift in the region,” and the administration sees them as reliable partners for advancing U.S. interests. This approach fits into the administration’s “Enlist and Expand” strategy, which focuses on partnering with like‑minded governments to counter Chinese influence, secure trade and investment opportunities, and pressure other countries to join a U.S.‑led bloc. The initiative is therefore designed not as a broad hemispheric coalition but as a curated alliance of governments aligned with Washington’s geopolitical and ideological goals.
Critics argue that the strategy is short‑sighted. The document warns that relying on personal or ideological alignment between leaders risks undermining long‑term relationships, especially in democracies where political power shifts frequently. It points to past examples, such as U.S.–Argentina relations, where close ties under one administration gave way to hostility under another. The text also notes that Trump’s approach has already triggered nationalist backlash in countries like Brazil and Canada, complicating U.S. influence rather than strengthening it. These patterns raise concerns that the Shield of the Americas could generate similar resistance and weaken U.S. standing over time.
The initiative also enters an already crowded landscape of regional organizations. The document highlights that more than 40 multilateral bodies operate in the Americas, creating opportunities for governments to “forum shop” for institutions that match their political preferences. Adding another ideologically driven alliance risks further fragmentation and reduces the ability of any single body to address collective challenges such as migration, security, or economic instability. The creation of ad hoc groups without mechanisms for long‑term coordination, the document argues, can undermine regional integration rather than strengthen it.
Mar 05, 2026 at 02:35 PM EST
FEMA staff describe ‘relief’ after Noem’s departure
A Federal Emergency Management Agency official said morale inside the agency has lifted following the announcement that Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem will leave her post at the end of March. Speaking to Newsweek's Leonardo Feldman, the FEMA source said Noem’s tenure brought added layers of bureaucracy that slowed internal operations, describing the environment as burdened by “more bureaucratic” processes and “a lot of red tape.”
According to the official, Noem’s exit is widely viewed inside FEMA as “a breath of relief,” with employees hoping the agency will receive the same level of attention and resources that Immigration and Customs Enforcement has enjoyed under the administration. The comments reflect broader tensions within the Department of Homeland Security, where different components have experienced uneven levels of support and visibility during Noem’s leadership.
Mar 05, 2026 at 02:33 PM EST
Mullin says he spoke with Trump after DHS announcement
Senator Markwayne Mullin said Thursday that he is still coordinating directly with President Donald Trump following the announcement that he will replace Kristi Noem as Secretary of Homeland Security. Speaking briefly with reporters, Mullin emphasized that he and the president “still got to communicate” as the transition begins, adding that they would “get on the same page and do the things we need to do.”
Mullin confirmed that he and Trump had already discussed the decision before the White House released its statement, though he suggested the news reached him only moments before it became public. “Yeah, the president and I already talked. Obviously. The statement already went out,” he said. “But we need to talk with the president… and we’re going to get on the same page.”
He added that he learned of his appointment “a little before you guys did."

Trump fires Noem, taps Sen. Mullin as homeland security secretary
sources.text:
U.S. President Donald Trump announced Thursday that Markwayne Mullin will take over as secretary of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security, replacing Kristi Noem in a major leadership change tied to the administration’s immigration policies.
"I am pleased to announce that the Highly Respected United States Senator from the Great State of Oklahoma, Markwayne Mullin, will become the United States Secretary of Homeland Security (DHS), effective March 31, 2026," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Noem will serve as "Special envoy for The Shield of the Americas," Trump said.
Noem, a former governor of South Dakota, became one of Trump's most high-profile Cabinet secretaries with social media posts that portrayed immigrants in harsh terms, highlighting cases of alleged criminal offenders and using vitriolic language. She faced criticism in January when she quickly labeled two U.S. citizens fatally shot by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis as committing "domestic terrorism."
Videos that emerged after the deaths undercut the assertion by Noem and other Trump officials that the two deceased - Renee Good and Alex Pretti - were violent aggressors. The public backlash for deaths led the Trump administration to move to a more targeted approach to immigration enforcement in Minnesota after months of sweeps through U.S. cities that led to violent clashes with residents opposing the crackdown. Democrats in the U.S. House of Representatives moved to impeach Noem and at least two Republicans in Congress called for her to lose her job after the incidents.
During congressional hearings in March, Democrats and some Republicans criticized Noem for her approach to the immigration crackdown and management of DHS, including concern over a $220 million ad campaign that heavily featured Noem. The staffing change raises questions about whether the Trump administration could seek to intensify its mass deportation push or retreat to a more targeted approach.
Under Noem's leadership, masked immigration agents surged into Los Angeles, Chicago and Washington, D.C., scouring neighborhoods and Home Depot parking lots in search of possible immigration offenders. The popularity of Trump's immigration approach fell as agents detained U.S. citizens and tear-gassed streets in an attempt to drive up deportations, which last year fell short of the administration's goal of 1 million per year.
While Noem, 54, served as a prominent proponent of Trump's agenda, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, a long-time Trump aide, controls Trump's immigration policy. Noem was quickly confirmed to lead the 260,000-employee Department of Homeland Security in January 2025 after Trump took office.
On social media, she referred to immigrants convicted of crimes as "scumbags" even as the number of non-criminals arrested by immigration authorities rose under Trump. She joined immigration enforcement operations on the ground in New York City and visited a maximum-security prison in El Salvador where Venezuelan immigrants deported by the Trump administration were being held without charges or access to lawyers.
The number of migrants caught trying to illegally cross the U.S.-Mexico border plummeted under Trump's restrictive policies, a steep drop after high levels of illegal immigration under former President Joe Biden, a Democrat.
Noem, reflecting Trump's agenda, also took steps to cut legal immigration programs and increase vetting. She ended several Temporary Protected Status programs that provided work permits to hundreds of thousands of immigrants from Venezuela, Haiti and other nations, drawing legal challenges.
After an Afghan immigrant was accused of attacking National Guard members in Washington, D.C., Noem said she recommended that Trump place "a full travel ban on every damn country that’s been flooding our nation with killers, leeches, and entitlement junkies."
Critics said Noem demonized immigrants and promoted an immigration enforcement strategy that targeted non-criminal, working immigrants and families. During Noem's tenure, the number of deaths in immigration detention rose to a two-decade high while staff in DHS oversight offices were slashed sharply.

sources.news_title: Trump names Oklahoma Sen. Markwayne Mullin as new DHS secretary
sources.text:
Kristi Noem to step down as DHS Secretary; Trump names Sen. Markwayne Mullin successor
WASHINGTON (TNND) — President Donald Trump announced that U.S. Sen. Markwayne Mullin of Oklahoma will become the next Secretary for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), effective March 31, 2026.
In a statement posted to Truth Social, Trump said current DHS Secretary Kristi Noem will transition to a new role as Special Envoy for “The Shield of the Americas,” a Western Hemisphere security initiative the administration plans to formally unveil Saturday in Doral, Florida.
Deputy Secretary Troy Edgar, a Navy veteran, will replace Noem temporarily. While Mullin will need to be confirmed by the Senate to officially serve in the position, federal law states that he would be allowed to serve as active secretary while his nomination is "formally pending."
Mullin's nomination will go through the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. The panel is chaired by Kentucky Republican Sen. Rand Paul, whom Mullin recently criticized as a "freaking snake," in remarks to voters in Tulsa.
The comment came as Mullin described how Paul, who has frequently defected from his own party in foreign policy, federal spending and other matters, proposes legislation that could tank a bigger package, such as appropriations bills and a farm bill.
"Rand Paul’s a freaking snake. And I understand completely why his neighbor did what he did. And I told him that to his face," Mullin said, according to Oklahoma conservative talk show host David Arnett. Mullin was referring to a 2017 attack where Paul was assaulted by a neighbor who tackled him and broke several of his ribs in a lawn maintenance dispute.
Due to a new state law in Oklahoma, Gov. Kevin Stitt will appoint a Senator to fill Mullin's seat, meaning a special election will not take place.
Trump praised Noem’s tenure at DHS, citing what he described as “spectacular results,” particularly on border enforcement.
Under Noem’s leadership, more than 2 million people self-deported in 2025, emphasizing Trump’s mass deportation agenda during his second term.
During a 30-minute speech to the Sergeant Benevolent Association Major Cities Conference in Nashville on Thursday, Noem did not mention her removal. No one asked Noem about the news during a question-and-answer session either.
On social media, Noem responded to the news of her ouster.
"Thank you @POTUS Trump for appointing me as the Special Envoy for the Shield of the Americas. @SecRubio and @SecWar are incredible leaders and I look forward to working with them closely to dismantle cartels that have poured drugs into our nation and killed our children and grandchildren. The Western Hemisphere is absolutely critical for U.S. security. In this new role, I will be able to build on the partnerships and national security expertise, I forged over the last 13 months as Secretary of Homeland Security," Noem wrote on X.
We have made historic accomplishments at the Department of Homeland Security to make America safe again: we delivered the MOST secure border in American history, 3 million illegal aliens have left the U.S., we have located 145,000 children, FEMA delivered disaster relief at a 100% faster rate, we ushered in the golden age of travel, saved the American taxpayer $13 billion and revitalized the U.S. Coast Guard," she added.
Mullin, a Republican who has served 10 years in the U.S. House of Representatives and three years in the Senate, is expected to oversee border security, immigration enforcement, and domestic threat prevention at DHS.
The president described Mullin as a strong advocate of his America First agenda, highlighting his background as a former professional mixed martial arts fighter and his role as the only Native American currently serving in the Senate.
Mullin told reporters that he found out a little bit before "you all" did.
I am super excited about this opportunity. It came at, not a complete surprise, but it came at a little bit of surprise for us.”
In a post on X, Mullin thanked the people of Oklahoma for allowing him to serve for the past 13 years.
I am grateful to President Trump for nominating me to lead the U.S. Department of Homeland Security. I look forward to earning the support of my colleagues in the Senate and carrying out President Trump’s mission alongside the department’s many capable agencies and the thousands of patriots who keep us safe every day," Mullin wrote.
Mullin also said he looks forward to supporting Trump's mission to "safeguard the American people and defend the homeland."
White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt said the administration will work with the Senate to confirm Mullin "as quickly as possible." She also thanked Noem for her service and welcomed her to her new role.
"President Trump is grateful to @KristiNoemfor helping usher in the most secure border in American history, and he looks forward to her continuing to serve in her new important role as Special Envoy for the Shield of the Americas. The White House will work with the Senate to confirm the extraordinarily qualified Senator @MarkwayneMullin as the next Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security as quickly as possible. President Trump’s immigration agenda is keeping our borders secure and deporting illegal alien criminals from our country, and it will continue without interruption," Leavitt said.
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Noem had done “a great job setting us up for success” and commended her “excellent” work on border security.
“The president is making a change,” Hegseth said during a news conference Thursday at U.S. Central Command. “We all serve at the pleasure of the president."
When asked if he worried about the safety of America’s homeland during the war, Hegseth said he did not, adding that he felt Mullin “will do a fantastic job.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he looks forward to working with Noem in her new role with The Shield of Americas, which he described as a new security initiative comprised of 13 countries.
Kristi has achieved incredible results as Secretary of Homeland Security and will be a tremendous asset in our effort to promote security and prosperity in the Western Hemisphere," Rubio wrote on X.
DHS oversees agencies including U.S. Customs and Border Protection, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the Transportation Security Administration, the Secret Service, and the Federal Emergency Management Agency.
Noem served as the eighth Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security.
Before joining Trump’s Cabinet, Noem served as the 33rd Governor of South Dakota, becoming the first woman elected to lead the state. She was re-elected in 2022 with the largest vote total in South Dakota history.
Before her time as governor, Noem represented South Dakota as its sole member of the U.S. House of Representatives. She also served in the South Dakota state legislature earlier in her political career.
Earlier this week, Noem was in the hot seat, testifying before the Senate Judiciary Committee and the House Oversight Committee - her first congressional appearance since the shooting deaths of two U.S. citizens.
During her hearing with the Judiciary Committee, Noem defended her department’s immigration enforcement actions.
In her opening statement, Noem credited President Donald Trump's leadership and Homeland Security personnel with what she described as historic results, including steep declines in border encounters, record-low apprehensions, and successful arrests and deportations.
"Thanks to President Trump's leadership and the hard work of the men and women of DHS, our department has delivered historic results and has made our community safer," Noem said. "Since the start of President Trump's second term, daily encounters along the southwest border declined by 96% compared to the Biden administration's daily average."
She also highlighted efforts to locate missing unaccompanied migrant children and curb drug trafficking, while warning that ICE officers are facing what she called an escalating threat, including sharp increases in death threats and assaults.
Additionally, Noem criticized Senate Democrats over the ongoing DHS funding impasse, saying the standoff is straining critical security missions and harming department employees. She thanked DHS staff for continuing their work during the dispute.
During her hearing with the Oversight Committee, Republicans focused their questioning on sanctuary cities and the defense of Noem from Democrat-led claims, as Democrats focused their questioning on the tactics used by ICE agents to detain individuals and the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.
Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin accused Noem of engaging in a cover-up with the investigations into the deaths of Good and Pretti during his opening statement.
"Rather than work with state and local authorities to solve these homicides, you barred Minnesota's investigators from the crime scenes. You're denying them access to all the evidence that you have about the deaths of their citizens. It smells like a cover-up, and it makes me wonder who the real domestic terrorists are," Raskin said.
In her own opening statement, Noem accused Raskin of lying and focused her remarks on the Angel Families, who she said need their stories told.
In a later exchange, Raskin repeatedly asked Noem whether she still thought Good and Pretti were domestic terrorists. After their deaths, Noem had accused both victims of trying to commit domestic terrorism.
"Based on what you know today, Madam Secretary, were Renee Good and Alex Pretti domestic terrorists?" Raskin asked.
"Congressman, what happened in Minnesota in those two incidents was an absolute tragedy," Noem responded, explaining that the investigations into their deaths remain pending.
Raskin continued to ask Noem the question, asking her why she did not wait for more evidence before making those claims. Noem offered condolences to the victims' families but did not apologize for the remarks, once again referring to the investigations.
On Jan. 7, ICE agents shot and killed the mother of three, Renee Good. On Jan. 24, Customs and Border Protection officers fatally shot Alex Pretti, who was filming enforcement operations. The deaths sparked protests and renewed calls for oversight of DHS actions.
Noem and other administration officials initially described the shootings as defensive actions — a characterization sharply disputed by critics.
In an effort to tone down tensions, President Trump dispatched border czar Tom Homan to Minneapolis to oversee operations, who has since announced that Operation Metro Surge is coming to an end.
Noem said about 650 investigators remain in Minnesota as part of a broader fraud probe.
__________________
Editor's note: The Associated Press and The National News Desk's Caitlyn Frolo contributed to this article.

sources.news_title: Donald Trump fires Kristi Noem at DHS. Here's who will replace her
sources.text:
Donald Trump fires Kristi Noem at DHS. Here's who will replace her
Washington - President Donald Trump fired Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem on Thursday after months of controversy, including the fatal shootings of two U.S. citizens by federal officers in Minneapolis and lawmakers' questions over a $220 million advertising contract.
The Republican president will tap Oklahoma Senator Markwayne Mullin to replace her by the end of the month, he said on his Truth Social platform on Thursday. The appointment would require U.S. Senate confirmation.
Noem, a former governor of South Dakota, became one of Trump's most high-profile Cabinet secretaries with social media posts that portrayed immigrants in harsh terms, highlighted alleged criminal offences and used vitriolic language.
Her departure, after emerging as the face of an aggressive immigration crackdown that had grown unpopular according to recent polling, could allow Trump to reset his approach on immigration policy, a centerpiece of his agenda.
Shortly after Trump announced Noem's replacement, she posted on X: "We have made historic accomplishments at the Department of Homeland Security to make America safe again."
During congressional hearings this week, Democrats and some Republicans criticized Noem for her approach to immigration enforcement and management of her department, including concern over a $220 million advertising campaign that featured Noem heavily and had been awarded to two longtime Republican operatives without a standard bidding process.
Noem's personal life also came under scrutiny, with a Democratic lawmaker on Wednesday asking whether she had a sexual relationship with top aide Corey Lewandowski. Both are married.
Noem called the question from U.S. Representative Sydney Kamlager-Dove "tabloid garbage." Lewandowski did not respond to a Reuters request for comment.
Trump told Reuters on Thursday that he did not sign off on the ad campaign, which prominently featured Noem and included a scene of her on horseback at Mount Rushmore, in her home state of South Dakota.
In one congressional hearing this week, Noem told Republican U.S. Senator John Kennedy that Trump had approved the ad campaign.
First Senate-confirmed cabinet member fired in Trump 2.0
Noem is the first Senate-confirmed member of Trump's Cabinet to be removed this term. In Trump's 2017-2021 term in office, 14 confirmed Cabinet appointees, who serve in the line of succession to the presidency, quit or were fired.
Noem faced criticism in January when she quickly accused two U.S. citizens fatally shot by federal immigration agents in Minneapolis of "domestic terrorism." Videos that emerged after the deaths undercut the assertion by Noem and other Trump officials that the two deceased - Renee Good and Alex Pretti - were violent aggressors.
The public backlash over the deaths led the Trump administration to adopt a more targeted approach on immigration enforcement in Minnesota, after months of sweeps through U.S. cities that sparked violent clashes between federal agents and residents who opposed the crackdown.
Two Trump administration officials, speaking on the condition of anonymity to discuss a personnel matter, said the fallout over the fatal shootings, the $220 million contract, the mismanagement of DHS and the allegations of the affair all contributed to her firing.
Democrats in the U.S. House of Representatives moved to impeach Noem, and at least two Republicans in Congress called for her to lose her job after the shootings in Minnesota.
Trump said on Truth Social that Noem would be appointed envoy to a planned summit in Miami to reinforce his Western Hemisphere policies.
Within minutes of Trump's post about her replacement, Noem spoke at a law enforcement event in Tennessee for 40 minutes but did not mention her departure.
Noem was aware she would be removed before she spoke at the event, one of the officials and another person familiar with the matter said, both of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity.
They added that Lewandowski was also expected to leave the department. DHS and the White House did not immediately comment when asked about Lewandowski's future.
Strong embrace of Trump's hardline immigration approach
Mullin, who spent a decade in the House of Representatives before becoming a senator in 2023, also supports Trump's hardline immigration agenda.
Speaking to reporters on Thursday, Mullin said he had not been expecting the call from Trump. He described Noem as a friend and said he had not had a chance to call her yet.
"She was tasked to do a very difficult job," Mullin told reporters.
Democrats in Congress have blocked funding for DHS since mid-February, saying federal immigration enforcement must be reformed.
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer said Noem's firing would not be enough to break the stalemate.
"The problems at ICE transcend any one person," he told reporters. "The president has to end the violence and rein in ICE."
Trump's immigration approach lost popularity as agents detained U.S. citizens and tear-gassed streets in an attempt to drive up deportations, which last year fell short of the administration's goal of 1 million per year.
While Noem, 54, served as a prominent proponent of Trump's agenda, White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, a longtime Trump aide, controls Trump's immigration policy.
Noem was quickly confirmed to lead the 260,000-employee department in January 2025 after Trump took office. On social media, she referred to immigrants convicted of crimes as "scumbags" even as the number of non-criminals arrested by immigration authorities rose under Trump.
She joined immigration enforcement operations on the ground in New York City and visited a maximum-security prison in El Salvador where Venezuelan immigrants deported by the Trump administration were being held without charges or access to lawyers.

❓WHAT HAPPENED: President Donald J. Trump announced a change in the position of United States Secretary of Homeland Security, effectively firing Kristi Noem via Truth Social.
👤WHO WAS INVOLVED: Kristi Noem, Markwayne Mullin, and Donald Trump.
📍WHEN & WHERE: The announcement was made via Truth Social, effective March 5, 2026.
💬KEY QUOTE: “Markwayne will make a spectacular Secretary of Homeland Security.” – Donald Trump
🎯IMPACT: Markwayne Mullin will take over as Secretary of Homeland Security, while Kristi Noem transitions to a new role as Special Envoy for The Shield of the Americas.
President Donald J. Trump announced a significant leadership change in his administration. Markwayne Mullin, a United States Senator from Oklahoma, is set to become the new Secretary of Homeland Security, effective March 31, 2026.
The news comes after Kristi Noem, who will move into a new role as Special Envoy for The Shield of the Americas, became embroiled in a $220 million ad-buying campaign scandal, covered here by The National Pulse.
Trump praised Noem for her service, particularly her accomplishments on border security. He expressed gratitude for her contributions, stating, “I thank Kristi for her service at ‘Homeland.'”
Markwayne Mullin, who served 10 years in the House of Representatives and three in the Senate, has been recognized as a “MAGA Warrior.” Trump emphasized Mullin’s dedication to advancing the America First agenda and his commitment to securing the border.
When Sen. Markwayne Mullin joins President Trump’s cabinet, Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt will appoint a temporary replacement within 30 days.
The appointee must be a Republican who has been a registered Oklahoma voter in that party for at least the previous five years, and they must sign a written promise not to run for the seat in the upcoming election. This interim senator would serve until the winner of the regular November 2026 Senate election is sworn in early 2027. Since Mullin’s seat is already scheduled for the 2026 ballot (where he had been seeking his first full six-year term), no separate special election is needed.

sources.news_title: Trump says he's replacing Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem
sources.text:
Trump fires Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Thursday fired his embattled Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, after mounting criticism over her leadership of the department, including the handling of the administration’s immigration crackdown and disaster response.
Trump, who said he would nominate Oklahoma Republican Sen. Markwayne Mullin in her place, made the announcement on social media after Noem faced a two-day grilling on Capitol Hill this week from GOP members as well as Democrats.
Noem’s departure marks a stunning turnaround for a close ally to the president who was tasked with steering his centerpiece policy of mass deportations. But she appeared to increasingly become a liability for Trump, with questions arising over her spending at her department and over her conduct in the aftermath of the shooting deaths of two protesters in Minneapolis earlier this year.
Trump said Noem “has served us well, and has had numerous and spectacular results (especially on the Border!).” He said he was making her a “Special Envoy for The Shield of the Americas,” a new security initiative that he said would focus on the Western Hemisphere.
Noem, who appeared at a law enforcement event in Nashville, Tennessee, moments after Trump’s announcement, did not address her ouster there. She read from prepared remarks and was not asked by attendees about the development.
Later, in a social media post, she thanked Trump for the new appointment and touted her accomplishments as secretary.
“We have made historic accomplishments at the Department of Homeland Security to make America safe again,” she wrote.
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said the administration will work with the GOP-led Senate to get Mullin, whom she called “extraordinarily qualified,” confirmed to lead DHS “as soon as possible.”
The administration’s immigration crackdown faced criticism, especially in Minnesota
Noem is the first Cabinet secretary to leave during Trump’s second term. Her tenure looked increasingly short-lived after hearings in Congress this week where she faced rare but blistering criticism from Republican lawmakers. One particular point of scrutiny was a $220 million ad campaign featuring Noem that encouraged people in the country illegally to leave voluntarily.
Noem told lawmakers that Trump was aware of the campaign in advance, but Trump disputed that in an interview Thursday with Reuters, saying he did not sign off on the ad campaign.
Noem has faced waves of criticism as she’s overseen Trump’s immigration crackdown, especially since the shooting deaths of the two protesters in Minneapolis at the hands of immigration enforcement officers. In the immediate aftermath of the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, Noem portrayed both of them as aggressors, contradicting widely viewed videos and descriptions of their deaths from bystanders. She declined to apologize for her description over two days of Congressional testimony.
The former South Dakota governor was also criticized over the way her department has spent billions of dollars allocated to it by Congress.
Her department, DHS, has been at the center of a funding battle in Congress over immigration enforcement tactics and has been shut down for 20 days, although many of the employees are continuing to work, often without pay.
Even before Noem’s appearance before key congressional committees this week, Republican lawmakers had been anticipating the secretary’s eventual ouster, particularly after her handling of the immigration enforcement crackdown in Minneapolis.
As they tried to end the ongoing Homeland Security shutdown, Senate Republicans had noted privately to Democratic senators that Noem was likely on her way out and that that should prompt Democrats to move forward with agreeing to fund the department again, according to two people familiar with the discussions.
Democrats did not see that as an actual concession by Republicans, considering Noem was becoming a political liability for the GOP, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss private negotiations.
Aside from immigration, Noem also faced criticism — including from Republicans — over the pace of emergency funding approved through the Federal Emergency Management Agency and for the Trump administration’s response to disasters.
Critics welcomed Noem’s departure. Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey wrote “good riddance” on social media, a sentiment echoed by Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer.
Some immigration activists questioned whether her departure would change the execution of an immigration agenda that they fundamentally disagree with.
“This is not accountability, just a reshuffling of the enablers of the agenda of President Trump,” said Vanessa Cárdenas, Executive Director of America’s Voice, an advocacy group. She said Noem’s tenure was “marked by cruelty.”
Gregory Bovino, a Border Patrol official who was elevated under Noem’s watch to lead immigration crackdowns in cities including Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis, was one of the few who applauded Noem’s tenure.
“She is the best Secretary I ever worked for, period. The others weren’t even close. Noem is the ultimate patriot,” Bovino told The Associated Press.
DHS leadership changes come at a pivotal time
Mullin would need to be confirmed by the Senate, but under a federal law governing executive branch vacancies, he would be allowed to serve as an acting Homeland Security secretary as long as his nomination is formally pending.
Voting in the Senate just after Trump’s announcement, Mullin said he has “no idea” how quickly his nomination will move.
“The president and I are good friends. So we look forward to working closer with the White House, and obviously I’m gonna be over there a lot more,” he said.
Mullin would take over the third-largest department in government that has responsibility for carrying out Trump’s hardline immigration agenda. And he would assume the role at a pivotal time for that agenda.
Immigration enforcement during the first year of Trump’s administration was largely defined by high-profile, made-for-social-media operations with flashy names, often led by Bovino, who reported directly to Noem. Noem herself often went out on those operations, riding along with officers when they went out to make arrests.
But those high-profile operations in places like Los Angeles, Chicago and Minneapolis often led to clashes with activists and protesters that were captured on video and drove opposition to the president’s immigration agenda.
That culminated with the shooting deaths in Minneapolis after which Trump shuffled leadership of the operation. The number of officers there was drawn down shortly after.
Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick contributed.

sources.text:
President Trump on Thursday fired Kristi Noem as DHS Chief and immediately announced her replacement.
Senator Markwayne Mullin (OK) will become the next Secretary of Homeland Security effective March 31.
Markwayne Mullin will have to be confirmed by the Senate.
“I am pleased to announce that the Highly Respected United States Senator from the Great State of Oklahoma, Markwayne Mullin, will become the United States Secretary of Homeland Security (DHS), effective March 31, 2026. The current Secretary, Kristi Noem, who has served us well, and has had numerous and spectacular results (especially on the Border!), will be moving to be Special Envoy for The Shield of the Americas, our new Security Initiative in the Western Hemisphere we are announcing on Saturday in Doral, Florida,” Trump said.
“I thank Kristi for her service at “Homeland,”” Trump said on Truth Social.
“Serving 10 years in the United States House of Representatives, and 3 in the Senate, Markwayne has done a tremendous job representing the wonderful People of Oklahoma, where I won all 77 out of 77 Counties — in 2016, 2020, and 2024! A MAGA Warrior, and former undefeated professional MMA fighter, Markwayne truly gets along well with people, and knows the Wisdom and Courage required to Advance our America First Agenda,” Trump said.
“As the only Native American in the Senate, Markwayne is a fantastic advocate for our incredible Tribal Communities,” he said.
“Markwayne will work tirelessly to Keep our Border Secure, Stop Migrant Crime, Murderers, and other Criminals from illegally entering our Country, End the Scourge of Illegal Drugs and, MAKE AMERICA SAFE AGAIN. Markwayne will make a spectacular Secretary of Homeland Security. Thank you for your attention to this matter!” Trump said.
Earlier Thursday The Wall Street Journal, citing advisors, reported that President Trump was gearing up to fire Kristi Noem.
President Trump is preparing to fire Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, according to advisers.
The president has already been asking aides and congressional Republicans for names of potential replacements, the advisers said.

Alongside the announcement of Noem’s ouster, Trump said he would tap Sen. Markwayne Mullin, R-Okla., to replace her, elevating a fiercely loyal first-term senator.
“I am pleased to announce that the Highly Respected United States Senator from the Great State of Oklahoma, Markwayne Mullin, will become the United States Secretary of Homeland Security (DHS), effective March 31, 2026,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
He added that Noem, who he said “has served us well,” will take over a new role called “Envoy for The Shield of the Americas.” He described the position as one that will lead “our new Security Initiative in the Western Hemisphere.”
Trump spoke to Noem about the job switch Thursday afternoon, according to two people familiar with the conversation. Noem is traveling outside Washington.
An administration official told NBC News that Trump decided to fire Noem because of “a culmination of her many unfortunate leadership failures including the fallout in Minnesota, the ad campaign, the allegations of infidelity, the mismanagement of her staff, and her constant feuding with the heads of other agencies, including CBP and ICE.”
The official added: “Kristi’s drama sadly overshadowed and distracted from the Administration’s extremely popular immigration agenda, which will continue full force.”
Noem thanked Trump on X for her new position and touted her tenure as DHS secretary.
"In this new role, I will be able to build on the partnerships and national security expertise, I forged over the last 13 months as Secretary of Homeland Security," she added before she included a list of "historic accomplishments," at the department.
Corey Lewandowski, a close aide and adviser to Noem, is also expected to leave DHS, according to an administration official.
Lewandowski, who was one of the first staff members on Trump’s 2016 campaign for president, faced scrutiny from lawmakers over his role at the department, including over whether he had the power to approve grants and contracts. In congressional hearings this week, Noem, who is married, faced questions about their personal relationship.
Mullin told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday that he was “super excited about this opportunity” and that it was “not a complete surprise.”
He added, “The president and I, as you guys know, we’re great friends, and we get along great. I look forward to working with him in his Cabinet. Of course, we’ve still got to go through this little thing called confirmation, and we’re going to get started on it right away.”
Mullin was at a Senate Republican lunch Thursday when he appeared to get a phone call, then “abruptly” got up and rushed out of the room — leaving a “full plate of food behind,” according to Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Miss., who said it raised suspicion among Republicans that something was afoot.
Mullin was spotted leaving the lunch using one hand to press the cellphone to his ear and the other to cover his mouth, as if he was trying to shield the conversation from reporters, and then ducked into the leadership office of Sen. John Barrasso, R-Wyo., just around the corner from the room where the GOP lunch was being held.
Mullin later said the phone call came from the White House switchboard, so he didn't see Trump's name pop up on the caller ID.
“I’ve got to be honest with you, I wasn’t expecting the call today,” he said.
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt called Mullin "extraordinarily qualified" on X and said the White House will work with the Senate to confirm him "as quickly as possible."
Mullin, a former MMA fighter, served for a decade in the House before he won a 2022 special election to the Senate. If he is confirmed as DHS secretary, Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt would be required to choose another Republican to fill the vacancy until the November midterm elections. Because Mullin’s Senate term expires this year, state law notes, there wouldn’t be a special election to replace him.
Shortly after Trump’s post Thursday, Noem delivered the keynote address at the Sergeants Benevolent Association Major Cities Conference in Nashville, Tennessee, and did not address that she would be stepping down this month.
“I appreciate your wisdom and your advice as we continue to develop trainings and insight into how leadership can work together to make good decisions and to break down the silos between agencies so that we can work together in better ways than we have in the past,” she told law enforcement officers.
Noem has been at the forefront of Trump’s signature policy agendas: deporting immigrants, restricting immigration and clamping down on the U.S.-Mexico border. She is the first Cabinet secretary to step down in Trump’s second term. Last year, Mike Waltz left his Cabinet-level post as national security adviser after Trump nominated him to become ambassador to the United Nations.
Noem's place in the administration became increasingly unstable after federal agents shot and killed two U.S. citizens during immigration operations in Minneapolis, her relationship with the Coast Guard, the only branch of the military under her command, began fraying and she made comments this week before lawmakers that rankled Trump.
In the congressional hearings Tuesday and Wednesday, lawmakers questioned Noem about the $200 million ad campaign she oversaw that urged anyone in the U.S. illegally to deport voluntarily. The ad campaign, which was conducted mostly in English, featured Noem. According to AdImpact, an ad-tracking firm, DHS has spent almost $80 million to air the ads since the start of 2025, not including the cost of production.
Noem told the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday that Trump approved the multimillion-dollar ad campaign, a claim the White House denied.
“POTUS did not sign off on a $220 MILLION dollar ad campaign. Absolutely not,” a White House official told NBC News on Thursday.
At the Senate and House hearings this week, Noem also faced questions from lawmakers about the administration’s actions in Minneapolis. The deployment of thousands of federal troops to conduct immigration enforcement activities, using at times brutal tactics, has led to intense bipartisan criticism of Noem’s leadership of DHS.
Noem declined to apologize for calling Renee Good and Alex Pretti, two Americans who have been killed by federal agents, “domestic terrorists,” though she conceded that investigations into the two deaths continue.
Republican Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska called for Noem to step down in January, with Tillis telling reporters he couldn’t “think of any point of pride over the last year” of her tenure.
Before she served in the Trump administration, Noem was the governor of South Dakota.
